title: Tinjauan Literature Sistematis: Dampak Transformasi Digital terhadap Kinerja ESG
summary: Digital transformation significantly impacts various aspects of life, including the business and financial sectors. There are concept that is gaining popularity in the business world is Digitalization and ESG, which emphasizes the importance of digital, environmental, social, and corporate governance factors in investment decisions. In this context, ESG performance is crucial for determining a company's sustainability and long-term value. This study utilizes a literature review with a bibliometric analysis approach. The findings reveal that research in fintech, ESG, and digital transformation are interconnected and integrated. However, compared to other financial topics, this area remains relatively under-researched, particularly concerning ESG in SMEs.

title: Does sustainable finance strengthen corporate governance? Evidence from ASEAN banks
summary: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractThe growing global demand for the integration of strong corporate governance in the banking industry is essential for enhancing financial performance. However, the interactive role of sustainable finance in strengthening governance mechanisms remains relatively underexplored. This study aims to examine whether adopting sustainable finance practices strengthens corporate governance mechanisms in the banking sector in ASEAN countries during the period 2018–2022. Utilizing the Fixed Effects Model, this study presents a notable finding. The results indicate that the interaction between management scores and green bonds has a positive and significant effect on Return on Assets, whereby a 5% increase in green bonds exposure raises ROA by 0.248, but exerts a negative effect on Return on Equity, with a decrease of 0.340 for every 1% increase. In contrast, the interaction between shareholder scores and green bonds has a negative and significant impact on ROA, with a decline of 0.223 for each 5% increase, while positively influencing ROE by 0.222 for every 1% increase. This study confirms that green bonds asymmetrically moderate the relationship between corporate governance and banking performance, in which management-oriented governance enhances asset efficiency but suppresses ROE, whereas shareholder-oriented governance reduces ROA while improving ROE. Conceptually, green bonds function as a balancing mechanism between corporate governance and banking performance, whereby managerial governance improves asset efficiency at the expense of equity returns, while shareholder-based governance enhances ROE with the trade-off of lower ROA.

title: IMPACT OF EXTERNAL AUDIT CHARACTERISTICS ON EARNINGS MANAGEMENT IN LISTED CONSUMER GOODS COMPANIES IN NIGERIA
summary: This study examines the impact of external audit characteristics on earnings management in listed consumer goods companies in Nigeria. Specifically, it investigates whether audit firm size, audit tenure, auditor type, and joint audit arrangements significantly influence earnings management, while controlling for firm size, firm age, leverage, and sales growth. Anchored on agency theory, information asymmetry theory, signalling theory, stakeholder theory, institutional theory, and the policeman theory, the study adopts a quantitative ex-post facto research design within a positivist framework. Panel data were obtained from audited annual reports of 16 consumer goods firms listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) over the period 2006–2022. The data were analysed using panel regression techniques to test the hypothesised relationships and the empirical results reveal that external audit characteristics collectively have a statistically significant effect on earnings management (Wald χ² = 24.95; p = 0.0016). However, the individual effects of audit firm size, audit tenure, auditor type, and joint audit were all negative but statistically insignificant, suggesting that these audit attributes do not independently constrain earnings management in the Nigerian consumer goods sector. The study concludes that while external audit characteristics jointly matter in explaining earnings management behaviour, their standalone effects are weak in the presence of firm-specific factors. The recommends the need for stronger institutional enforcement and complementary governance mechanisms to enhance the effectiveness of external audit structures in curbing earnings manipulation in emerging markets.

title: Microplastic contamination in agricultural systems: impacts on plant productivity, economic losses, and supply chain resilience
summary: Microplastics (MPs) have transitioned from a predominantly marine concern to a defining threat facing terrestrial agroecosystems, where croplands now function as one of the largest global reservoirs of plastic particles. This review synthesizes evidence to construct an integrated narrative that links the entry of MPs into farmland with declining plant productivity, quantifiable economic losses, and the erosion of agricultural supply chain resilience. The synthesis is based on a documented search of Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar covering January 2018 to March 2026, with explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria reported in Section 1.1. Sources, fate and soil-phase processes are treated in condensed form, because they are already covered comprehensively elsewhere; we retain only the evidence that propagates into crop, economic and supply-chain outcomes. Building on these soil-level disturbances, we evaluate the phytotoxic consequences for crops, spanning inhibited germination, impaired root architecture, reduced photosynthetic efficiency, disrupted nutrient acquisition, and the uptake and translocation of nano-sized particles into edible tissues. A central contribution of this review is the explicit coupling of these biophysical impacts to their economic and systemic dimensions, because recent global meta-analyses estimate that MP-induced photosynthetic suppression alone may reduce staple crop production by tens to hundreds of millions of tons annually, translating into substantial revenue losses, quality downgrading, remediation expenditure, and heightened exposure of food supply chains to shocks. Rather than reporting these modelled outputs at face value, we dissect the inferential chain that produces them, from effect size to biomass to harvestable yield to price, and we identify the assumptions at each step that determine whether the resulting figures are decision-grade. We complement the global estimates with farm-level cost–benefit evidence showing that the private returns to plasticulture remain positive while the contamination externality contributes under one percent of the accounted benefits of current management, which explains the persistence of practices that degrade the productive base. Throughout, illustrative case studies from China, Chile, Australia, and Europe are embedded within each thematic section rather than treated in isolation, demonstrating how local contamination patterns propagate into landscape- and market-scale consequences. We further appraise mitigation and remediation options, ranging from source reduction and material substitution to biochar amendment, and we assess emerging governance instruments such as the FAO Voluntary Code of Conduct and circular-economy regulation. Finally, we identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning the calibration of field-realistic dose–response relationships, the construction of decision-grade economic estimates, and the severe geographical imbalance of the evidence base, in which South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America are collectively represented by a small fraction of published field studies, and we outline research priorities to safeguard soil health and food security. The review argues that microplastic contamination should be reframed not merely as an ecotoxicological problem but as a slow-onset stressor with strategic implications for the stability of global food systems.

title: Does Overvaluation Predict Earnings Management? Evidence on the Agency Costs of Overvalued Equity in a Frontier Market
summary: Most of the accounting literature on emerging markets asks whether capital markets reward high-quality earnings. This paper reverses the question and asks whether market valuation shapes subsequent reporting. Using 4981 firm-year observations for 619 non-financial Vietnamese listed firms, with misvaluation measured from 2016 to 2024 and earnings management from 2017 to 2025, and measuring misvaluation through the Rhodes-Kropf et al. decomposition alongside five Tobin’s Q-based measures, we find that overvaluation in one year predicts more aggressive earnings management in the next. The estimate is positive and significant at the one percent level for all six measures in specifications that absorb firm and year fixed effects, control for prior accrual behaviour, and use standard errors clustered by firm. A one within-firm standard deviation increase in the firm-specific error raises absolute discretionary accruals by 6.6 percent of their within-firm standard deviation. The accruals are directional, and the relation runs through magnitude rather than incidence: overvaluation predicts how large income-increasing accruals are once reported, but neither the probability that they are reported nor the probability of falling in the upper tail of the accrual distribution. The relation weakens as leverage rises, which is consistent with creditor monitoring; formal interaction tests do not support the corresponding predictions based on firm size or state ownership. A firm-block bootstrap that reproduces both first-stage models raises the standard error by 23 percent but leaves the confidence interval clear of zero, and randomisation inference across 1999 permutations places the estimate well outside the placebo distribution. The evidence is substantially stronger for within-firm variation than for cross-firm comparison: in a propensity-score matched sample the estimate is not distinguishable from zero and covariate balance is unsatisfactory. The design is observational and does not identify a causal effect. Because equity-based compensation and an active market for corporate control are largely absent in this setting, the findings indicate that the association does not depend on the channels through which price pressure is conventionally assumed to operate, although they do not identify the channel that does operate.

title: Sustainable Corporate Loans: A Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
summary: ABSTRACT This paper presents a systematic literature review of sustainable corporate loans (SCLs), including green loans and sustainability‐linked loans, to synthesise current academic knowledge and outline future research directions. Using a PRISMA protocol and a bibliometric analysis of 102 peer‐reviewed articles published in AJG‐ranked journals (3 and above) between January 2009 and May 2025, the review examines publication trends, theoretical perspectives, methodological approaches, thematic patterns and research gaps. The literature shows rapid growth after 2020, with substantial regional concentration in China, the United States and Europe. Stakeholder theory is the most frequently invoked explicit theoretical lens, although many studies do not anchor their analysis in a clearly stated theory. Quantitative designs prevail, but longitudinal, mixed‐method and experimental approaches remain scarce. Four main themes emerge: borrower ESG and financial outcomes, lender incentives and risk management, loan contract features, and macroeconomic implications. Key gaps relate to causal identification, ESG metric standardisation and borrower–lender dynamics in emerging markets.

title: Financial Technology, Digital Transformation and Higher Education Outcomes: Evidence from Saudi Arabia in Comparative Perspective (2019–2023)
summary: Using comparative data for Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States over 2019–2023, this study examines conditional associations between Financial Technology (FinTech), digital infrastructure, and higher-education outcomes. The empirical unit is the country-year, yielding 25 observations (5 countries × 5 years). The empirical strategy combines descriptive cross-national benchmarking with parsimonious two-way fixed-effects panel models. The baseline models use the FinTech Penetration Index (FPI) internet penetration, Gross Domestic Product GDP per capita, and public education spending, with country and year fixed effects. The estimates show mixed conditional associations across enrollment, graduation, and administrative cost per student and are interpreted cautiously because only five countries are observed. Financial inclusion is treated as a theoretical mechanism that is not directly measured in the present panel. The study therefore provides a transparent comparative Financial Educational Technology (FinEdTech) framework while emphasizing the limits of inference from a small national panel.

title: Gender diversity in South African audit committees and financial reporting quality: A critical mass analysis
summary: This study explores the relationship between gender diversity in South African audit committees and financial reporting quality (FRQ) of non-financial companies listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange from 2020 to 2024. A quantitative approach was employed to investigate these relationships, utilising an ex post facto design to collect data from the Osiris database and integrated annual reports. Gender diversity within audit committees was assessed using several measures: dummy variables indicating whether an audit committee had one female director (ACFD1) or two or more female directors (ACFD2), as well as the proportion of females on the committee (ACGD) and its square (ACGD²). FRQ was assessed using earnings management (EM), evaluated through accrual earnings management (AEM) and real earnings management (REM). The study applied both linear and curvilinear models, using fixed-effects models and Two-Stage Least Squares to test the hypotheses. The regression results revealed that ACFD1 had an insignificant negative impact on AEM and an insignificant positive impact on REM. In contrast, ACFD2 showed a significant negative impact on both AEM and REM. Additionally, ACGD had a significant positive impact on AEM, while ACGD² exhibited a significant negative impact. For REM, ACGD also had a significant positive effect, whereas ACGD² demonstrated a significant negative impact. These results indicate that audit committee gender diversity has an inverted U-shaped effect on both AEM and REM. The study's inverted U-shaped results align with critical mass theory, which suggests that a balanced representation of female directors (between 40% and 60%) can reduce earnings manipulation and enhance FRQ. Furthermore, these results provide a strong business case for increasing female representation to critical-mass levels, thereby minimising EM. Theoretically, this research underscores the importance of critical mass and collective action when examining the economic benefits of gender diversity in audit committees. Regulators are encouraged to consider audit committee gender diversity beyond mere numbers.

title: Does public attention effectively reduce climate risk vulnerability? Evidence from 30 Chinese Provinces from 2012 to 2022
summary: Purpose In the context of intensifying global climate risks and increasingly frequent extreme weather events, enhancing climate adaptation capacity and strengthening risk management have become urgent tasks for governments and the public. The purpose of this study is to examine the effect of public climate attention on provincial climate vulnerability across Chinese provinces. Members of the public are key social actors in climate policy: their awareness and risk perception can prompt action that reduces vulnerability to climate risks. Design/methodology/approach China is a geographically diverse country and faces both coastal risks, such as sea-level rise, and inland challenges, such as droughts and extreme weather. Using provincial panel data in China from 2012 to 2022, this paper measures public climate attention through Baidu search volumes of climate-related keywords and constructs a climate risk vulnerability index based on exposure, sensitivity and resilience. A two-way fixed-effects model is used to examine the relationship between public climate attention and climate risk vulnerability, as well as its underlying mechanisms. Findings The findings show that climate risk vulnerability in China follows a spatial pattern, being low in the southeast and high in the northwest, with an overall declining trend over time. Public climate attention significantly reduces climate risk vulnerability, a conclusion that holds across several robustness tests. The effect is strongest for resilience, followed by sensitivity and weakest for exposure. It is primarily attributable to the promotion of green innovation and renewable energy. This mitigating effect is particularly pronounced in provinces with lower levels of green finance development. Originality/value This study offers four key innovations. First, it constructs a quantitative measure of public climate attention using the Baidu Index and develops a multidimensional provincial climate risk vulnerability index, providing a new empirical basis for climate risk perception research. Second, it reveals that higher public climate attention significantly reduces regional climate risk vulnerability, adding a behavioral perspective to climate governance studies. Third, it identifies the structural pathways through which attention affects vulnerability, mainly by strengthening adaptive capacity. Finally, it uncovers transmission mechanisms, showing that public climate attention promotes green innovation and improves energy structure and efficiency.

title: Environmental, Social, and Governance Reporting and Firm Value: The Moderating Role of Corporate Transparency in Latin America
summary: This research analyzes the relationship between ESG performance and firm value in Latin America, considering the role of corporate transparency. We used a panel data structure with a sample of 330 companies observed annually from 2014 to 2024. The results demonstrate a negative relationship between ESG performance and Tobin’s Q, suggesting that stakeholders tend to interpret sustainability initiatives as short-term costs rather than strategic investments. However, this relationship changes when corporate transparency is incorporated, indicating that consistent, credible disclosure helps the market reinterpret these actions and value them positively. When ESG is broken down, the environmental and social components explain the initial negative effect, while governance is not significant. Reputation, as reflected in Big Four audits, does not change this relationship. The findings suggest that ESG influence is indirect and depends on how companies communicate it to the market. Therefore, companies must strengthen their ESG strategies with more effective transparency policies, since stakeholders require integrated non-financial information to avoid short-term biases.

title: The Empirical Impact of Social Investment on the Corporate Cash Holdings of South African Financial Institutions
summary: This study examined the effect of social investment on corporate cash holdings in South African financial institutions, addressing a gap in the existing literature, which has largely concentrated on developed countries and non-financial industries. The research provides empirical data on the association between social investment and corporate cash reserves within an emerging-market financial sector. A quantitative, positivist, and deductive research design was adopted, using secondary data collected from 18 South African financial institutions for the period spanning 2015 to 2024. The data were obtained from the Thomson Reuters Eikon and World Bank databases, and the analysis employed the system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator to control for dynamic connections and potential endogeneity issues. The findings showed a highly significant negative connection between social investment and corporate cash reserves, indicating that firms holding larger cash reserves tend to allocate fewer resources to social investment activities. The results also revealed a strong inverse connection between social investment and cash holdings, suggesting that firms with higher cash balances invest less in social initiatives. These findings indicate a misalignment between the goals of corporate social responsibility programmes and liquidity management strategies in South African financial institutions. The study emphasizes the importance of incorporating social investment into corporate cash holding policies and recommends that managers direct cash reserves towards socially beneficial initiatives rather than maintaining excessive cash balances. By offering data from an emerging-market setting, the study contributes to the fields of sustainability and corporate finance and provides valuable insights for managers making financial and cash reserves decisions that enhance stakeholder value.

title: Institutional factors influencing the development of corporate social responsibility, taking into account the regional characteristics of Russia
summary: A quantitative assessment was conducted of the impact of key institutional factors – regulatory pressure, geographical specialization, and dependence on a single industry town – on the development and implementation of corporate social responsibility (CSR) practices in companies operating in the Far Eastern Federal District of Russia. Empirical Analysis was conducted using a dataset of the 22 largest companies in the region. The methodology includes fixed-effects regression analysis to assess the direct impact of factors, construction of regulatory pressure and geographical isolation indices, threshold regression to identify nonlinear dependencies, and structural equation modeling to test mediation hypotheses. The Results confirm the dual impact of regulatory pressure, which stimulates the environmental component of CSR (β = 0.21) but reduces social investments (β = –0.15) due to resource redistribution effects. It was found that geographical isolation and single-industry town status are significant determinants of increased local social responsibility (β = 0.11 and β = 0.17, respectively), with this influence being fully mediated by the need to obtain a “social license to operate”. For extractive companies operating in territories inhabited by indigenous peoples, a critical threshold of social legitimacy was identified (0.65 on the standardized scale), exceeding which significantly reduces operational risks. The institutional environment acts as a key mediator through which CSR practices affect the long-term financial sustainability of business (indirect effect β = 0.38; 88% of the total effect). Overall, the effectiveness of CSR in peripheral regions is determined not by the volume of investments but by the degree of their adaptation to local institutional conditions. This confirms the need for a contextual approach to sustainable development management.

title: Research on the Impact of Carbon Accounting Information Disclosure on Corporate Reputation
summary: At present, the concept of environmental protection has become deeply rooted in people's minds, and enterprises should therefore assume their social responsibilities. Corporate reputation, as an important intangible asset, is increasingly attracting the attention of stakeholders. This article mainly analyzes the significance of carbon accounting information disclosure on corporate reputation, and explores the process mechanism by which carbon accounting information disclosure affects corporate reputation. It provides a reference for enterprises to optimize their information disclosure strategies and enhance their reputation levels in the context of low-carbon transformation.

title: EXTENDING THE CONTEXTUALIZED RESILIENCE-AGILITY ARCHITECTURE: TEMPORAL AMBIDEXTERITY IN CONSUMER GOODS SUPPLY CHAINS
summary: Consumer goods firms face a persistent tension between supply chain resilience and operating efficiency. Existing resilience research explains many of the capabilities firms require, but provides less guidance on when those capabilities should be activated as disruption conditions change. This study addresses that temporal gap by extending the Contextualized Resilience-Agility Architecture (CRAA) through a temporal ambidexterity perspective. Using a sequential multi-method design, the study combines a comparative multiple-case analysis of five U.S. and Chinese consumer-goods firms with longitudinal analysis of the 2026 U.S. import environment. Phase I identifies four recurring resilience mechanisms: selective slack, digital visibility linked to executable options, appropriately distributed decision rights, and ecosystem-level coordination. Phase II shows that the value of these capabilities is time contingent because sensing, plan revision, decision authorization, and physical execution operate on different horizons while operational choices become progressively less reversible. The study develops temporal ambidexterity as the ability to advance, delay, accelerate, or sequence supply chain commitments under uncertainty. It further introduces temporal selective slack, forecast revision capacity, temporal optionality, and temporal alignment to explain how firms preserve and exercise operational choices within narrowing decision windows. The resulting framework extends CRAA from a capability architecture toward a temporally contingent explanation of resilience and reframes resilience as the ability to preserve efficiency while committing neither too early nor too late.

title: An Information Systems Model for Cloud-Based Accounting Adoption and MSME Financial Reporting Compliance
summary: This study proposed an information systems model to investigate the relationships among cloud-based accounting adoption, financial reporting compliance, and reporting quality in Indonesian micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). A total of 320 records were collected and processed through data cleaning, coding, normalization, and indicator standardization before being operationalized into latent constructs based on expert-defined measures. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 4.0 was employed in the analysis. The measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and convergent validity, satisfying recommended thresholds for Cronbach's Alpha, Composite Reliability, and Average Variance Extracted, while the structural model showed acceptable explanatory power. The results reveal that compliance with standards positively influences financial reporting quality (β = 0.32). Cloud-based accounting adoption also significantly mediates and strengthens this relationship (β = 0.45). MSMEs combining regulatory compliance with cloud accounting achieved the highest reporting quality. These findings extend the information systems literature by demonstrating the enabling role of cloud accounting in transforming compliance into improved reporting outcomes, while offering practical implications for policymakers, MSME support agencies, and software developers seeking to enhance financial accountability and digital transformation.

title: Blockchain for Transparency in Sustainable Apparel Supply Chains
summary: The increasing demand for transparency in global apparel and textile supply chains has accelerated interest in blockchain as a digital solution to improve traceability, stakeholder trust, and sustainability. However, existing research has primarily emphasized blockchain’s technological capabilities while offering limited insight into how governance mechanisms shape the relationship among transparency, trust, and sustainability. Addressing this gap, this study investigates blockchain-enabled transparency through a qualitative cross-case analysis of sixteen documented transparency initiatives within the apparel and textile industry. Secondary empirical evidence was synthesized from peer-reviewed journal articles, industry reports, international organizations, and a non-governmental organization (NGO) transparency assessment using a structured analytical coding framework informed by blockchain affordance theory, interorganizational trust theory, accountability theory, and sustainability governance literature. The findings demonstrate that blockchain consistently enhances supply chain transparency by improving traceability, information visibility, and provenance verification; however, transparency alone does not generate stakeholder trust or measurable sustainability outcomes. Instead, trust emerges when blockchain-enabled transparency is supported by governance mechanisms, such as third-party verification, certification systems, auditing practices, and clearly defined accountability arrangements. Sustainability benefits are similarly indirect, arising through improved governance, organizational decision-making, and stakeholder collaboration rather than through blockchain technology itself. This study contributes to the literature by reconceptualizing blockchain-enabled transparency as a governance capability rather than solely a technological capability and proposes an integrated governance pathway linking blockchain affordances, transparency mechanisms, governance arrangements, stakeholder trust, and sustainability outcomes. The findings provide practical guidance for apparel brands, manufacturers, policymakers, and certification bodies seeking to strengthen transparent and sustainable supply chain governance.

title: Environmental proactivity relates to perceived sustainability performance through green innovation and resource efficiency in Vietnamese manufacturing
summary: Manufacturers in emerging economies face simultaneous pressure to reduce environmental impacts and preserve operating competitiveness, yet a proactive environmental orientation does not automatically translate into broad sustainability gains. Drawing on the natural-resource-based view, dynamic capability theory, and institutional theory, this study examines two internal conversion mechanisms green innovation capability and resource efficiency and the contextual role of perceived environmental institutional pressure. Survey data from 278 knowledgeable informants in Vietnamese manufacturing firms were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, bootstrap mediation and moderation tests, robustness analyses, and 10-fold cross-validation. The findings show that environmental proactivity is associated with perceived sustainability performance both directly and indirectly through two complementary routes: renewal through green innovation capability and operational optimization through resource efficiency. Institutional pressure is positively associated with green innovation capability, but it does not significantly amplify the proactivity–innovation relationship. The study contributes by specifying how strategic environmental intent is converted into sustainability-oriented capabilities rather than treating orientation as a self-executing resource. For managers and policymakers, the results support a balanced portfolio that combines innovation capability building with resource-efficiency improvement, while using external pressure together with technical support, implementation capacity, and green-finance access.

title: CORPORATE GOVERNANCE AND FRAUD PREVENTION: THE ROLE OF AUDITORS IN UNCERTAIN REGULATORY ENVIRONMENTS
summary: This study investigates the interplay between corporate governance mechanisms and fraud prevention, focusing on the moderating role of auditors in an uncertain regulatory environment. Drawing on an ex post facto research design, we analyse secondary data from 10 consumer goods firms listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group between 2015 and 2023. Corporate governance is operationalised through board size, board independence, and audit committee size, while auditor quality is captured by engagement of Big 4 versus non-Big 4 audit firms. Fraud prevention is proxied by the incidence of financial restatements. Descriptive statistics reveal that most firms maintain mid-sized boards with over 50 % independence and engage Big 4 auditors, yet restatements remain rare. Correlation and multiple regression analyses indicate that neither governance structures nor auditor engagement, alone or in interaction, significantly predict restatement occurrences (Adjusted R² ≈ 0.01). These findings suggest that structural governance metrics and auditor labels are insufficient to capture the complexity of fraud prevention. We concluded that qualitative assessments of internal controls, investment in technology-driven audit techniques, enhanced audit committee expertise, and improved regulatory transparency are critical for strengthening fraud-prevention mechanisms in emerging-market contexts.

title: Balancing Efficiency and Human Oversight in AI-Driven ESG Audits: The Roles of AI Automation and Decision Making
summary: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) audits has created new opportunities to enhance corporate governance through faster and more consistent assurance processes. However, concerns remain regarding accountability, transparency, and the role of human oversight in AI-assisted auditing. Prior research has predominantly examined AI adoption in traditional financial auditing, leaving its role in the more qualitative and judgment-intensive context of ESG assurance comparatively underexplored, particularly with respect to how AI decision-making authority should be balanced against human oversight. This study examines the effects of AI automation and AI decision making on audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency, while assessing the mediating role of human oversight. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were collected from 150 professionals involved in ESG audit-related functions (including ESG auditors, compliance officers, sustainability managers, and AI governance analysts) across private, public, and non-governmental organizations, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling via professional networks, audit forums, and LinkedIn ESG groups. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that AI automation significantly improves audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency. Similarly, AI decision making within governance structures exerts positive effects on all three outcome dimensions. Furthermore, human oversight partially mediates these relationships, strengthening the overall impact of AI on ESG audit outcomes. These results suggest that AI enhances ESG auditing effectiveness, but its benefits are maximized when supported by strong governance and human supervision. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled ESG assurance by demonstrating the importance of balancing technological efficiency with accountability and transparency in corporate governance.

title: STRENGTHENING DIGITAL CITIZENSHIP COMPETENCIES OF PPKn MASTER STUDENTS AS PROSPECTIVE UMKM ENTREPRENEURS: A LEGAL-NORMATIVE REVIEW AND ACTUALIZATION OF PANCASILA ECONOMICS
summary: Digital transformation has reshaped citizenship, higher education, and MSME entrepreneurship in Indonesia. In this context, Master’s students of Pancasila and Civic Education should no longer be positioned merely as prospective educators or academics, but also as digital citizens with the potential to become actors of people-centered entrepreneurship grounded in Pancasila values. The state has established a regulatory framework for the facilitation, protection, and empowerment of MSMEs, including the strengthening of the digital ecosystem; however, digital literacy, digital ethics, legal awareness, and social justice orientation remain substantive challenges (Government of the Republic of Indonesia, 2021; Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia, n.d.; “Transformasi Digital UMKM Indonesia,” n.d.). This study aims to analyze a model for strengthening the digital citizenship competence of Master’s students in Pancasila and Civic Education as prospective MSME entrepreneurs through a juridical-normative approach and the perspective of Pancasila economics. The study employs qualitative library research with juridical-normative, philosophical, and conceptual approaches. Data were collected through document studies of legislation, recent academic publications, institutional reports, and relevant scholarly articles, and were analyzed using content analysis and thematic interactive analysis. The findings show that strengthening digital citizenship competence among Master’s students in Pancasila and Civic Education should be constructed through four integrated dimensions: digital-regulatory literacy, digital ethical-participatory capacity, digital social entrepreneurship capacity, and a Pancasila-based economic justice orientation. From the normative perspective, the national legal framework has opened legal and institutional space for MSME digitalization, yet it has not been fully translated into postgraduate civic education designs that prepare students as sovereign, responsible, and justice-oriented actors in the digital economy. This study offers a novelty by reconstructing digital citizenship competence not merely as the ability to use digital media safely and ethically, but as a form of civic-economic competence that connects digital rights, constitutional responsibilities, business legal compliance, and the praxis of people-centered economy in digital spaces (“Strengthening Citizenship Skills,” n.d.; “Strategi Penerapan Ekonomi Pancasila,” n.d.; “Implementasi Pancasila dalam Kebijakan Ekonomi,” n.d.; Government of the Republic of Indonesia, 2021; Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia, n.d.). The study concludes that Master’s students in Pancasila and Civic Education occupy a strategic position as agents of civic entrepreneurship reform who can bridge civic education, economic law, and national MSME empowerment. The implications point to the need for curriculum reformulation, stronger campus policies, and the development of a Pancasila-based digital civic entrepreneurship learning ecosystem.

title: Beyond conventional ESG: configurational synergies and path effects on the return resilience of infrastructure REITs
summary: As sustainable development has gained increasing prominence, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues have become an important research topic in the field of infrastructure real estate investment trusts (Infra-REITs). However, the three conventional ESG dimensions alone are no longer sufficient to fully explain the mechanisms through which ESG affects earnings resilience. Drawing on the operational characteristics of the Infra-REITs market, this study develops an “ESG+” analytical framework comprising two dimensions: underlying assets and capital markets. Using both questionnaire evidence and empirical data, it integrates fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) and necessary-condition analysis (NCA) to systematically identify the configurational paths through which multiple factors jointly shape the earnings resilience of Infra-REITs. To mitigate potential subjective bias, a LASSO regression model is further employed to identify key variables containing incremental predictive information and to conduct a complementary comparison with the configurational results. The results show that: (1) ESG elements such as green certification, energy efficiency, and social responsibility significantly enhance return resilience under specific contextual conditions, demonstrating strong multi-factor synergies; (2) project cash flow and energy efficiency emerge as core conditions across several configurations, underscoring the foundational role of operational performance in shaping Infra-REITs’ resilience; and (3) under imperfect legal and fiscal systems, market liquidity, pricing mechanisms, and information disclosure interact as critical complementary mechanisms that strengthen return stability. The findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of ESG–resilience linkages and provide theoretical and practical guidance for optimizing investment management and improving institutional design in the Infra-REITs market.

title: How Machine Learning Will Transform Supply Chain Management
summary: The Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, trade wars, and other events in recent years have disrupted supply chains and highlighted the critical need for businesses to improve planning in order to be more agile and resilient. Yet companies struggle with this challenge. One major cause is flawed forecasting, which results in delivery delays, inventory levels that are woefully out of sync with demand, and disappointing financial performance. Those consequences are hardly surprising. After all, how can inventory and production decisions be made effectively when demand forecasts are widely off?

title: Corporate social responsibility as a strategic resource: examining the mediating role of corporate reputation in securing competitive advantage
summary: Introduction Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is increasingly described as a strategic intangible resource. Yet, the mechanism by which it converts into competitive advantage (CA) remains underspecified, and evidence from the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies is limited. Drawing on stakeholder theory and the resource-based view (RBV), this study examines corporate reputation (CR) as the pathway that links CSR to CA in organizations operating in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Methods A cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Structured questionnaires were delivered to 200 managers using convenience sampling, with 150 valid responses retained. The measurement quality was evaluated using exploratory factor analysis, average variance extracted (AVE), composite reliability, and the Fornell–Larcker criterion. We addressed common method variance through procedural remedies and Harman’s single-factor test. Hypotheses were tested using ordinary least squares regression and bootstrapped mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 resamples), controlling for firm age, organization size, and organization type. Results CSR was positively associated with CR ( B = 0.746, p < 0.001) and CR was positively associated with CA ( B = 0.403, p = 0.001). The total effect of CSR on CA was positive and significant ( B = 0.526, p < 0.001); however, the direct effect was not significant once CR entered the model ( B = 0.226, p = 0.061). The indirect effect through CR was significant [ B = 0.301, 95% bootstrap CI (0.079, 0.507)] and accounted for approximately 57.2% of the total effect, indicating an indirect-only (full) mediation. Discussion The results suggest that CSR relates to competitive advantage mainly through corporate reputation, rather than directly affecting competitive position. Reputation therefore appears to operate as the conversion mechanism that translates stakeholder approval into a resource position that is valuable, rare, and difficult to imitate.

title: Mapping the Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainable Finance: A TCCM-Driven Bibliometric Analysis and Conceptual Framework
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and sustainable finance are increasingly intersecting, yet research at their intersection remains fragmented and theoretically underdeveloped. This study combines bibliometric analysis with the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework to examine 61 PRISMA-screened articles retrieved from Web of Science. No publication-year restriction was applied; the included corpus spans 2021 to July 2025. Publication output within the corpus increased from seven articles in 2023 to fifteen in 2024, while the 2025 count covers only the period up to the July search date. China accounts for the largest share based on the corresponding author’s country. Stakeholder Theory is the most frequently applied theoretical lens (10 studies), followed by the Resource-Based View (7 studies) and Institutional Theory (5 studies). Within the thematic map, ESG and artificial intelligence occupy the motor-theme quadrant, whereas green finance lies in the emerging-or-declining quadrant. Building on the TCCM synthesis, the study develops a dual-level conceptual framework grounded in the Resource-Based View and Institutional Theory. The framework proposes that AI-related capabilities may contribute to sustainability outcomes through absorptive capacity, green-innovation processes, and supply-chain efficiency, and positions institutional quality, environmental uncertainty, ownership type, and industry competitiveness as boundary conditions. Overall, the study provides a structured theoretical synthesis and a theory-informed agenda for future research at the AI-sustainable finance nexus.

title: Driving sustainable banking performance: the roles of digital transformation, FinTech adoption, and financial inclusion under regulatory environment moderation
summary: Purpose With sustainability becoming a global priority, financial institutions increasingly use FinTech to support sustainable performance within evolving regulatory environments. This study investigates how digital innovation, specifically FinTech Adoption and financial inclusion, is associated with firms' sustainable performance while examining the moderating role of the regulatory environment in shaping these relationships. It also offers insights into how regulatory frameworks can support the use of digital tools to promote a more sustainable financial future. Design/methodology/approach This study employed a survey methodology to collect data from bank employees in Saudi Arabia. From a total of 402 survey responses, 385 were considered valid and used for analysis. The proposed relationships were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings The study revealed that digital transformation was significantly linked to sustainable performance, FinTech Adoption, and financial inclusion. Fintech Adoption was positively related to financial inclusion and sustainable performance. The moderation analysis showed that the regulatory environment strengthens the association between financial inclusion and sustainable performance. However, it does not significantly moderate the relationships between FinTech Adoption and sustainable performance or digital transformation and sustainable performance. Originality/value This study contributes a perspective by applying the Resource-Based View and Technological Innovation Systems frameworks to examine how internal capabilities and regulatory support are associated with sustainable performance. It also addresses a contextual gap by focusing on the Saudi banking sector under Vision 2030 reforms. The findings provide partial support for the moderating role of the regulatory environment, highlighting the complexity of regulatory influence.

title: Digital Transformation Disclosure and Green Technological Innovation Toward Sustainable Manufacturing: Evidence from Chinese Listed Firms
summary: Green technological innovation is important to the sustainable development of manufacturing. As a core driver of transition toward sustainable production patterns, green innovation helps firms reduce environmental externalities while maintaining economic competitiveness. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and the Knowledge-Based View, this study examines the association between digital-transformation disclosure and green technological innovation using 16,231 firm-year observations for Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2015 to 2022. Green technological innovation is measured by green patent applications, and the baseline specifications use negative binomial models with year and industry fixed effects, province-clustered standard errors, and a full control set that includes firm size. Digital-transformation disclosure is positively associated with green patent applications. Parallel-mediation estimates and province-clustered Bootstrap confidence intervals identify significant indirect effects through inter-organizational knowledge flow, R&D expenditure intensity, and the R&D personnel share. In terms of point estimates, the R&D personnel indirect effect is the largest of the three, followed by knowledge flow and R&D expenditure; however, only the R&D personnel versus R&D expenditure difference is statistically significant, and the three channels are better characterized as complementary. The difference between the knowledge-flow and R&D-expenditure effects is marginally significant. The hypothesized inverted-U moderating pattern of market competition is not statistically significant in the preferred specification with industry and year fixed effects. Split-sample estimates show directional heterogeneity across region, ownership, and firm size, but formal interaction tests do not reject equality of the digital transformation disclosure coefficients across groups. These results document robust associations rather than definitive causal effects and highlight the complementary roles of knowledge recombination, R&D expenditure, and technical personnel in green patenting. These findings carry implications for sustainability-oriented research and management practice by documenting channels through which digital-transformation disclosure is associated with green patent activity in the manufacturing sector.

title: Climate finance, innovation, and the low-carbon transition in Portugal: Evidence from a nonlinear ARDL approach
summary: Balancing economic development with environmental sustainability remains a critical challenge for many European economies pursuing low-carbon transitions. Although Portugal has made substantial progress in renewable energy deployment and technological innovation, the environmental impacts of economic growth, urbanization, and trade openness remain complex. They may exhibit asymmetric responses to policy and market shocks. Therefore, this study investigates the asymmetric and dynamic relationships among urbanization (URB), trade openness (TRD), economic growth (EG), renewable energy (RE), innovation (INNO), and carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions in Portugal using the Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag (NARDL) framework. Annual time-series data covering the period 1990–2023 were employed to examine both long-run and short-run asymmetries in the environmental effects of these macroeconomic factors. The empirical findings reveal that positive shocks in EG and URB significantly increase CO₂ emissions, whereas increases in RE consumption and INNO substantially reduce environmental degradation. TRD exhibits mixed effects; while trade expansion initially increases emissions through higher production activity, it contributes to long-run emissions reductions through technology diffusion and cleaner trade composition. The results further indicate that negative shocks to RE and INNO have disproportionately adverse environmental consequences, highlighting the fragility of sustainability gains. These findings demonstrate Portugal’s progress in aligning economic development with RE transition and INN-driven climate strategies. The study provides novel evidence on the asymmetric effects of economic and policy shocks on environmental quality. It offers policy recommendations that support the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 7, 9, 11, and 13.

title: Atlantica Cinemas Limited: Behind the Screens at a Small Business Audit
summary: ABSTRACT This CPA‐style case focuses on Atlantica Cinemas, an independent cinema chain operating in Atlantic Canada. Students are called upon to draft an audit planning memo that considers the nature of the company's operations, structure, and ownership. Several key financial reporting issues are also explored. This case is designed for capstone or early graduate‐level courses, as well as later portions of undergraduate audit and assurance courses where students have experience with financial reporting and assurance topics.

title: The impact of governance on strengthening audit practices and promoting financial transparency: an empirical investigation in the Iraqi business context
summary: This study examines the relationship between corporate governance mechanisms and financial disclosure among companies listed on the Iraq Stock Exchange. Drawing on agency theory and stakeholder theory, the study considers how internal and external governance arrangements influence transparency in an emerging market characterized by institutional and regulatory constraints. The study employs a quantitative research design based on firm-year data from 19 listed companies over the period 2018–2022, yielding 95 observations. Financial disclosure is measured using a structured disclosure index derived from annual reports. The governance variables include board structure, managerial ownership, ownership concentration, audit committee presence, remuneration committee presence, risk committee presence, and the external auditor’s opinion. The findings indicate that governance mechanisms linked to active monitoring, particularly audit and risk committees, are positively associated with financial disclosure. Remuneration committees and unqualified audit opinions also show positive relationships with disclosure, while ownership concentration is negatively associated with transparency. Board structure does not show a statistically significant effect, suggesting that formal board arrangements alone may not be sufficient to enhance disclosure in this context. The study contributes to the governance and disclosure literature by providing empirical evidence from the Iraqi business environment, where institutional constraints may shape the practical effectiveness of governance mechanisms. The results offer implications for regulators, policymakers, and boards seeking to strengthen financial reporting practices and improve investor confidence in emerging markets.

title: The Multiple Economic Value of Information in the Digital Economy: Toward a multidimensional framework for information, and artificial intelligence
summary: In the digital economy information has taken on the role of a key economic resource, even though its economic value does not have to be the same as its market price. The body of work in information economics has provided a number of important but mostly separate explanations of information asymmetry, uncertainty reduction, signaling, property rights, pricing, network effects, organizational information and intangible capital. The present paper looks at these contributions again by means of a qualitative, theory-focused review of the literature referred to in the source text and puts forward an integrative interpretation of informational value. It is argued that information should be regarded as a multidimensional economic resource whose value can at the same time include aspects relating to use, exchange, organization, network, social and temporal dimensions. Market price is thus only one possible form of informational value and not a complete measure of it. The digital economy makes this distinction more apparent since digital information can be copied and distributed at a very low marginal cost, can produce consumer and network benefits which are not entirely reflected in transactions, and can at the same time act as both a private asset and a shared resource. Artificial intelligence enhances these features by increasing the scale, speed and complexity of information processing. The paper does not assert that economics as a whole is inadequate; instead it maintains that the various theories of information should be taken into account together when the economic value generated by information as a whole is the object of analysis.

title: Research on the Impact of Digital Transformation on Innovation Performance in Manufacturing Enterprises
summary: This study investigates the impact of digital transformation on the innovation performance of listed manufacturing companies and explores the mediating mechanism of R&D expenditure. Utilizing a sample of Chinese firms, the empirical results demonstrate that digital transformation exerts a significantly positive impact on innovation efficiency and performance, with R&D expenditure serving as a critical bridging mechanism. This study enriches the existing theoretical framework, offering empirical evidence for digital strategies while suggesting future inquiries into firm heterogeneity.

title: Toward Sustainable Supply Chains: The Spillover Effects of Customer Environmental Disclosure on Supplier Carbon Emissions
summary: Supply chain decarbonization is essential for achieving corporate sustainability and broader climate goals, yet emission reduction across organizational boundaries remains difficult because lead firms and suppliers often operate under fragmented environmental information. Although environmental information disclosure (EID) is increasingly viewed as an important instrument for improving corporate transparency, existing research has primarily examined its consequences within firm boundaries, leaving its cross-organizational sustainability implications insufficiently understood. Drawing on signaling theory, this study examines whether customers’ environmental management disclosure is associated with upstream suppliers’ carbon emissions and conceptualizes the reduction of environmental information asymmetry as a key channel through which such disclosure may influence suppliers. Using a panel of 2213 supplier-year observations constructed from Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2022, we estimate fixed-effects panel regressions to examine the relationship between customer environmental disclosure and supplier carbon intensity. The results show that suppliers exposed to environmental information disclosure from at least one customer have approximately 10.95% lower estimated carbon emissions, while a one-point increase in the average environmental disclosure score of a supplier’s customer base is associated with approximately 2.96% lower estimated supplier carbon emissions. Further analyses show that disclosure strength does not significantly moderate this relationship, whereas the characteristics of disclosed information matter: positive environmental disclosure strengthens the negative association between customer disclosure and supplier carbon intensity, while negative disclosure weakens it. These findings extend research on environmental disclosure beyond the focal firm by documenting its association with environmental outcomes across supply chain relationships. They also suggest that customer disclosure may transmit clearer environmental signals, thereby contributing to more sustainable and resilient supply chains.

title: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Maturity Framework for Organizational Governance and Digital Transformation
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven digital transformation has become a strategic priority for organizations seeking to enhance competitiveness, operational efficiency, and innovation. However, existing AI maturity models primarily emphasize technological capabilities or data readiness, with limited integration of AI governance, risk management, ethics, organizational capabilities, and digital transformation into a comprehensive framework. This study aims to develop an Artificial Intelligence Maturity Framework to assess AI implementation maturity and support organizational digital transformation planning. The research employs a Framework Development Study approach by integrating Systematic Literature Review (SLR), Comparative Framework Analysis, Content Analysis, and Design Science Research (DSR). The framework is synthesized from existing AI maturity models, ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the OECD AI Principles, and recent studies on AI Governance and Responsible AI. The proposed Integrated AI Maturity Framework comprises a conceptual model, a matrix of dimensions and indicators, five maturity levels, a conceptual assessment instrument, and an AI implementation roadmap. The framework integrates nine dimensions: strategy, AI governance, AI risk management, AI ethics, data, technology, organizational capabilities and talent, innovation culture, and digital transformation. It provides a comprehensive conceptual foundation for evaluating and advancing sustainable AI implementation across diverse organizational contexts.

title: Towards a Next Generation of Accounting Information Systems: A Systematic Literature Review Approach
summary: Accounting Information Systems (AISs) are central to organisational decision-making, financial reporting, and regulatory compliance. Yet, the rapid digitalisation of financial operations has exposed these systems to cyber vulnerabilities, human errors, and inefficiencies in data management. To systematically examine these weaknesses, this paper employs a Systematic Literature Review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, analysing peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, and industry reports published between 2015 and 2025. The review identifies critical AIS vulnerabilities, including inadequate cyber controls, low human awareness of security risks, weak protection of digital assets, limited integration of risk management, absence of quantitative performance metrics, and restricted accessibility for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs). Based on these findings, a structured framework for next-generation AIS solutions is proposed, comprising real-time dashboards, cloud-based zero-trust architectures, hyper-automation, artificial intelligence-driven insights, blockchain, Internet of Things integration, self-healing systems, and adaptive risk engines. These interventions aim to strengthen data integrity, system resilience, regulatory compliance, and organisational agility, offering practical benefits to SMEs and large organisations operating in increasingly complex financial environments. Overall, the paper provides a comprehensive, evidence-based roadmap that bridges gaps in cybersecurity, operational efficiency, and decision-making within AIS, contributing valuable insights for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers seeking to modernise AISs while mitigating cyber, operational, and compliance risks.

title: Digital transformation and third places: Mapping public spaces in Bekasi Regency
summary: As an urban and industrial area, Bekasi Regency faces challenges in providing inclusive and multifunctional public spaces that support social interaction, community cohesion, and economic activities. The limited availability of formal public spaces has encouraged the informal use of vacant spaces by local communities, indicating a need for both formal and informal “third places.” This study aims to develop a spatial database of third places in Bekasi Regency, identify their distribution patterns, and evaluate user experience through a phenomenological approach. A mixed-methods approach was applied by integrating Geographic Information System (GIS)-based spatial mapping using data scraped from Google Maps with field observations and semi-structured interviews at 24 purposively selected locations. The study identified 136 third places, classified into Civic/Public Spaces (33.8%), Commercial Social Spaces (40.4%), Spiritual/Communal Hubs (7.4%), and Hybrid/Productive Spaces (18.4%). These locations are mainly concentrated in the West Cikarang, North Cikarang, and South Tambun corridors. Reclassification showed that 75.7% of third places operate informally, indicating that community demand for social spaces is largely met outside the formal planning system. Internet connectivity was also found to influence space selection among migrant workers, younger people, and informal business operators. Differences in spatial quality were observed between developed commercial areas and densely populated residential and peri-urban areas. These findings highlight the need to recognize informal and hybrid spaces in the Bekasi Regency Detailed Spatial Plan (RDTR) and strengthen public digital infrastructure to support inclusive urban development.

title: Impact of digital economy development on the sectoral employment structure in China: Analysis of direct and mediating effects
summary: The digital economy is a crucial driver of economic transformation, and exploring its impact on the employment structure is important for optimizing regional labor resource allocation. However, previous studies mostly focus on the growth patterns and macro effects of the digital economy, while neglecting its impact on employment structures across different sectors and its mediating effects. This study implements an evaluation system for the digital economy based on seven dimensions (mobile phone user numbers, internet broadband access volume, telecommunications business volume, express delivery business volume, Baidu search index for AI, number of AI enterprises, and the Digital Inclusive Finance Index) to analyze the spatiotemporal evolution of China's digital economy and its influence on the sectoral employment structure. The results indicate that the digital economy experienced continuous growth from 2011 to 2022, although the growth rate exhibits a downward fluctuating trend. The digital economy significantly promotes employment in the information and transportation, science-education-culture-health, and accommodation-catering services sectors, whereas it exerts a negative influence on the agriculture-forestry-animal husbandry-fishery and manufacturing sectors. Among the indicators analyzed, the number of mobile phone users per 100 people and Digital Inclusive Finance Index exhibit the most significant driving effects on employment restructuring, whereas internet broadband access volume per 100 people and the per capita express delivery business volume have relatively weak effects. Furthermore, the number of patents and proportion of tertiary industry serve as primary mediating variables influencing the employment structure through the digital economy. This study provides an important reference for optimizing employment structures and enhancing regional economic competitiveness.

title: Investigating The Influence of Digital Transformation, Budgeting and Budgetary Control on The Financial Performance of SMEs: A Critical Review
summary: This critical review evaluates the study by Ebhota et al. (2024) concerning the impact of digital transformation (DGT), big data analytics (BDA), customer experience (CUE), and budgeting and budgetary control (BBC) on the financial performance (FFP) of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging markets. Employing a critical literature review methodology, this paper assesses the original study's theoretical foundations, methodological rigor, and empirical claims. The analysis confirms that grounding the research in Dynamic Capability Theory effectively frames digital transformation as an evolving operational asset rather than a static IT expenditure. Furthermore, the underlying statistical models robustly validate that DGT, BDA, and CUE significantly enhance budgetary controls and financial performance. However, this critical review identifies notable limitations in the original manuscript, including a pronounced demographic sample bias toward highly digitized technology and financial sectors (67%), which limits generalizability to traditional resource-heavy industries, alongside significant typographical and statistical reporting errors in the text. Despite these flaws, the reviewed study offers a highly relevant, empirically backed framework demonstrating how modern SMEs must integrate digital capabilities with financial discipline to achieve sustainable growth

title: Smart Tourism Planning and Regional Competitiveness: Insights from Bekasi’s Digital Transformation
summary: The rapid advancement of information and communication technologies has profoundly transformed urban governance and tourism development worldwide, giving rise to the concepts of Smart City and Smart Tourism as integrated models of sustainable innovation. In Indonesia, several local governments have adopted Smart City initiatives to enhance public service quality and economic competitiveness. Among them, Bekasi Regency has emerged as one of the leading regions in formulating a comprehensive Smart Tourism planning framework. This study aims to examine the key dimensions of Smart Tourism planning in Bekasi by analyzing how digital transformation, governance innovation, and technological integration are embedded within the regional development agenda. Employing a qualitative approach that combines literature review and in-depth interviews with members of the Bekasi Smart City Council, this research utilizes thematic analysis through NVivo software. The findings indicate that technology and innovation form the core of Bekasi’s Smart Tourism planning, emphasizing three interrelated components: Smart Experience, Smart Business Ecosystem, and Smart Destination. The study also reveals that although digital infrastructure and public service systems have been significantly developed, challenges remain in data management, interoperability, and community digital literacy. It concludes that effective Smart Tourism planning should prioritize data-driven governance, cross-sector collaboration, and community empowerment to strengthen tourism competitiveness and ensure sustainable regional development.

title: Why Do Divergent States Converge? Polycentric Governance and the Political Formation of Jurisdictional REDD+
summary: Jurisdictional REDD+ is widely promoted as a mechanism to align forest conservation, and climate mitigation, through standardized readiness frameworks and multilevel governance, yet a persistent dilemma remains: how can politically divergent subnational states converge on the same international climate finance outcomes? This study addresses that question by comparing two contrasting Brazilian Amazon states that both secured funding under the REDD+ Early Movers (REM) program. Methodologically, the research employs comparative process tracing, drawing on 287 documents and 74 semi-structured interviews, and applies Van Evera's evidence tests to assess the strength of causal explanations for program approval. The results reveal five necessary conditions for REM financing, formal compliance with REDD+ Readiness requirements was neither necessary nor sufficient for success; instead, informal arrangements, historical political trajectories, paradiplomatic networks, and multilevel coalitions among social actors played a decisive role. These findings lead to the conclusion that jurisdictional REDD+ operates less as a hierarchical implementation of institutional models and more as a polycentric governance process emerging from dynamic interactions across governance scales. By reconstructing the causal mechanisms that link international climate finance to subnational forest politics, this study advances theoretical debates on climate finance while offering practical insights for policy design in heterogeneous political contexts.

title: Digital Risk Governance in Higher Education Digital Transformation: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Digital transformation strategies at universities present significant challenges regarding structure and strategy, especially in digital risk governance. A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines to examine how these risks are managed and identify the frameworks applied, particularly in contexts where the integration of emerging technologies reshapes organizational processes. Indexed databases (Scopus, Web of Science, and Dimensions) were examined, focusing on publications from 2019 to 2025. Following the removal of duplicates and the application of inclusion and exclusion criteria, 40 pertinent papers were identified through an iterative filtering process of key themes associated with the topic. The results illustrate the governance strategies implemented and the interaction of rules, standards, and management models in digital transformation strategy. The review identifies conceptual fragmentation across digital transformation, digital culture, risk governance, and smart university research, and proposes an integrative synthesis grounded in the reviewed corpus.

title: ESG Performance and Earnings Management: Evidence from Chinese Listed Firms
summary: This study examines whether prior environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance is associated with subsequent accrual-based and real earnings management among Chinese A-share listed non-financial firms over 2015–2024. The temporally ordered design measures ESG performance at t?1, earnings management at t, and background covariates at t?2, yielding earnings-management outcomes from 2017 onward. Accrual-based earnings management (AEM) is measured by the absolute value of Modified Jones discretionary accruals, while real earnings management (REM) is captured by a signed composite of abnormal production costs, operating cash flows, and discretionary expenses. ESG performance is measured using a composite constructed from eight rating providers. Pooled ordinary least squares (OLS) models include Hybrid Industry and Year fixed effects with firm-clustered standard errors. The results show that stronger prior ESG performance is associated with a lower subsequent magnitude of AEM and lower subsequent upward-directed REM. The COVID-19 phase analysis shows that neither the During–Pre nor the Post–Pre contrast is statistically significant for the ESG–AEM association, whereas the negative ESG–REM association is significantly more pronounced in the Post period than in the Pre period. The principal full-sample associations remain consistent across the robustness specifications. All findings are interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects.
